## Why it works

The comments count their own mistakes and add memory aids. The creator's pinned question, "Be honest, how many of these did you find yourself doing?", has 232 likes and 89 replies. The most-liked viewer comments are rhymes for item 2: "My dad told me...black on brass will save your ass." (728 likes) and "Black is Brass, Chrome is Common, Green is Ground.... how I was taught." (513 likes). A retired electrician corrects item 2's reason: "Reverse polarity does not affect how devices work, on the other hand safety is jeopardized because appliances, lights designed with switches to break(open) the hot wire." (509 likes). Others confess and tell what happened: "Pretty sure I made every mistake in this video." (65 likes), "We found a loose black burnt wire that partially melted the receptacle and the breaker didn't trip!!" (48 likes), and a mistake the video doesn't cover: "I started a small fire in my last house because I had no idea this was a thing." (21 likes, the broken-off tab on a split outlet). The pace is praised: "No 5 minutes of intro baloney, each tip was right to the point with no unnecessary jabber" (32 likes). Item one starts at 0:28; the pace is brisk (about 217 words a minute). What viewers did after: they say they re-did outlets, bought a torque driver or switched from the push-in holes to the screws.

## Doesn't transfer

- **Electricians named in the opening as people who get it wrong:** [0:11] "biggest mistakes that not only diyers make but also some electricians make". Ours never runs down the trade.
- **No power-off or verify-dead line anywhere** (eight items of outlet wiring): every Frederick script says breaker off, then prove it with a tester checked on a live outlet first, inside the first step that needs it.
- **Pointing at the footage:** [0:34] "now this is a 15 amp receptacle this is a 20 amp receptacle"; [2:47] "this hole right here"; [16:31] "then click on this video right over here"
- **First-person tests on camera:** [4:21] "show you with this torque screwdriver what that looks like"; [6:34] "and look at how easy I can remove this wire just by"
- **Money and links** (no money framing on this channel): [5:17] "this one is actually really good for the money" and [15:51] "I'll have links for"
- **His own preferences and brands** (name the part type from the brief): [12:10] "commercial grade or a GFCI which I highly recommend" and [14:43] "one here by Levitin"
- **Unsourced claims about the trade:** [6:08] "that causes that arcing it gets very hot and fires can happen so this is one of the number one service calls" and [6:14] "I myself and every electrician that I've personally talked to recommend". Ours gives the reason from the brief, not a poll of electricians.
- **"Do you see the issue?" asked of the footage:** [7:00] "do you see the issue with this". Ours asks about the viewer's own outlet, never about a picture.
- **Factual slips to check against the brief:**
  - [2:49] "that means that power is not only flowing into this receptacle the wrong way" (AC has no wrong way; the real danger, as the 509-like comment says, is that a lamp's switch then opens the neutral and leaves the socket shell live)
  - [4:16] "screws will need to be tightened down to between 9 and 14 inbs" ("inbs" is inch-pounds; the figure is the maker's, from the brief)
  - [1:51] "you can put 15 amp receptacles on a 20 amp circuit with 12 gauge wire" (true where the circuit has more than one outlet; a single 15 amp outlet alone on a 20 amp circuit isn't allowed; check against the brief)
  - [11:05] "a huge no no not only is this against code because no manufacturer allows for more than one wire" (some clamp-type devices are listed for two wires per terminal; the device's own marking decides)
- **A mistake the comments add, missing from the video:** the broken-off tab on a split outlet, which a 21-like comment says started a small fire. If the brief covers it, it's ours to explain.
